agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The probe texts look right: 800 reference solutions plus 184 loop-stop probes, about 205k tokens in total, well within limits. The last line above confirms the Let-mode probe ends naturally at the point where the model would need to produce the answer. This pass is again on the original model with no edits active. I'm requesting only logprobs and top-5, so the output stays small. For the reference texts, the outcome of interest is which token class first breaks. For the loop probes, it's the share where top-1 reproduces the gold digits: a value near 15% or more would make stopping loops worth pursuing, and a value near 3-5% would mean loops are mostly a symptom of problems the model can't solve anyway.

Now for the analysis. For the loop probes, I'll count how many greedy continuations reproduce the gold number, including that the number stops there. For the reference solutions, I'll tag each digit token as a result (after "=") or an operand, the latter subdivided into numbers from the problem and numbers from earlier lines. For each class I'll report how often the correct digit is the model's top digit. Then I'll find, per solution, which class has the first incorrect number. This tells me whether a correct prefix tends to break at choosing operands (planning/retrieval) or computing results (arithmetic). I'm comparing digits only among digit candidates in the top-5, so differences in wording style between references and the model don't get counted as errors.

Both results are informative. Stopping loops at their onset is not worthwhile: greedy reproduces the gold number in only 6 of 184 probes (3.3%), so loops are mostly a symptom of problems the model has already lost, with a payoff of under +1 point. I'm closing that line, even though it's the most visible failure. In reference-solution prefixes, arithmetic turns out to be fairly healthy, with result digits correct 92-94% of the time, and only 71 of 800 solutions break first at a result. The largest first break by far is the choice of which number from the problem to use next: 357 of 800 solutions break there, with the first digit correct only 78% of the time. So the main failure with a correct prefix is retrieving the right quantity, which fits the dropped entities and swapped quantities I saw when reading failures. Some of this is ambiguity in operand order, so I need to see how structured it is. I'll break retrieval accuracy down by whether the target number has already been used in the solution, and by its position in the problem. I'll also check what the model's wrong top digit points to. A strong bias, such as avoiding unused numbers or preferring recent ones, would suggest a specific attention mechanism to examine next. If errors look uniform, I'd treat them as general retrieval noise.

Retrieval errors are broad, not biased. Accuracy sits around 0.73-0.82 whether a number is fresh or reused, early or late in the problem, and the wrong digit points to fresh numbers (291), used numbers (211) and non-problem numbers (292) in similar amounts. So I can't fix one simple preference such as "ignores unused numbers"; part of this is also just legitimate differences in plan order. Retrieval is still the biggest failure class, and it depends on attention, so the natural next step is direct observation. I'll use a pass to record attention at the four full-context layers. For statistical power, I'll build two multi-turn texts of DEV problems with reference solutions, since this mode allows only two texts of up to 2,048 tokens each. Then, at each token just before an answer number, I'll measure per head how much attention lands on the correct source number in the problem, compared with other digits and with other parts of the text. If one or two heads concentrate on source numbers far above baseline, they're a specific retrieval circuit I can scale and test at several strengths, using the reference-digit metric. If no head does this, retrieval must happen in the sliding-window layers I can't observe, and I'd probe those by knock-out instead.
